summary: This informational document describes how TCP, MPTCP, SCTP, UDP and UDP-Lite expose their services to applications and how applications can configure and use these features. It is part of work on a more flexible transport API.

plainLanguage.summary: It is a catalog of what each of the main transport protocols can do for a program, so developers can choose the right one.

questions: what features do tcp and sctp provide to applications
what transport features do tcp and sctp provide
what is the difference between tcp sctp and udp for applications
what are the three passes in rfc 8303
subtitle: A catalogue of what TCP, MPTCP, SCTP, UDP and UDP-Lite offer applications, boiled down into protocol-independent transport features.

tldr.problem: Applications are tied to a specific transport protocol, which makes it hard for a transport services (TAPS) system to pick or switch protocols for them.
tldr.mechanism: The RFC works in three passes: it summarizes what each protocol's specifications say about interacting with applications, unifies these into categorized primitives, then lists the superset of transport features and which protocols provide each.
tldr.outcome: The result is a set of transport abstractions that can be exported in a TAPS API, and a basis for the minimal set of transport services end systems should implement.

facts.label: Protocols covered
facts.value: TCP, MPTCP, SCTP, UDP, UDP-Lite (plus LEDBAT)

today: RFC 8303 is an Informational snapshot of the IETF transport protocols as of its publication in February 2018. The metadata for this entry shows no RFC that obsoletes or updates it.

sections.title: Purpose and Scope
sections.content:
The document describes how transport protocols offer transport services, so that applications are no longer directly tied to one protocol. Pushing complexity into an underlying transport services (TAPS) system can reduce the effort for the programmer while keeping flexibility. It builds on the survey in RFC 8095 and complements RFC 8304, which covers the first step for UDP and UDP-Lite.

It covers TCP, MPTCP, SCTP, UDP and UDP-Lite, and defines a primitive to enable, disable and configure the LEDBAT congestion control mechanism. It is strictly based on parts of the specifications that describe what a protocol provides to an application. Port multiplexing is always assumed and not discussed, and parts stated as optional to implement are not covered.
sections.plainLanguage: The goal is to describe what each delivery service offers so a program can ask for features instead of naming a specific service.

sections.title: The Three-Pass Method
sections.content:
In pass 1 the relevant RFC text is discussed per protocol. In pass 2 that discussion is turned into primitives and events that are uniformly categorized across protocols, named in the form CATEGORY.[SUBCATEGORY].PRIMITIVENAME.PROTOCOL. In pass 3 the transport features are listed, with the protocols that implement each.

Some features only become visible when protocols are compared. TCP always does congestion control, for example, and only next to UDP, which has none, does it become a feature. The complete list is therefore available only after pass 3. A primitive is a local function call between an application and a transport endpoint, an event is a primitive invoked by the endpoint, and a connection is shared state of two or more endpoints.
sections.plainLanguage: First read what each service says about itself, then sort the answers into groups, then make one big checklist showing who offers what.

sections.title: What Each Protocol Exposes
sections.content:
For TCP, the primitives include Open (active or passive), Send, Receive, Close, Abort, and events such as user timeout and error reports, plus options such as disabling the Nagle algorithm and configuring authentication keys. TCP Fast Open lets an application hand over a message with the SYN, which may be delivered more than once. The urgent mechanism is excluded because RFC 6093 says new applications SHOULD NOT employ it.

MPTCP offers the same primitives as TCP, plus a way to turn MPTCP on or off and to manage addresses and subflows. SCTP has a much larger set: associations with multiple addresses, message delimiters, streams, optional unordered or partially reliable delivery, heartbeats, path switchover, stream schedulers and many tuning parameters. UDP and UDP-Lite are covered in RFC 8304.

LEDBAT is a congestion control mechanism rather than a transport protocol and has no primitives. Its TARGET queuing delay must be set to 100 ms or less and its Base_History SHOULD be 10. All tunable parameters except the unprescribed filter function are proposed to be exposed.
sections.plainLanguage: Some services only have a few simple buttons, like TCP, and some have a big control panel, like SCTP.

sections.title: The Resulting Transport Features
sections.content:
Pass 3 groups connection features into four stages: establishment (active creation of a connection), availability (preparing to receive connections), maintenance (adjusting or monitoring an open connection) and termination. Data transfer features cover sending, receiving and errors.

On the sending side the features range from reliably transferring a byte stream with congestion control (TCP) to reliably or unreliably transferring messages (SCTP) and unreliably sending messages without congestion control (UDP and UDP-Lite). SCTP alone offers a choice of stream, a choice of path, configurable message reliability and a choice between ordered and unordered delivery. TCP closes only one direction on a local close, so it may still receive data afterwards. Receiving covers getting a stream of data, getting whole messages and information about partial message arrival.
sections.plainLanguage: The big checklist says, for every feature, which services have it, such as getting messages in order or sending without waiting for a reply.

sections.title: Security and Method Notes
sections.content:
Authentication, confidentiality protection and integrity protection are transport features according to RFC 8095, but they are generally provided by a layer on top of the transport protocol. They are therefore not considered here, with the exception of the native authentication of TCP and SCTP, to which the security considerations of RFC 5925 and RFC 4895 apply. Guidance for UDP usage is in RFC 8085. No IANA actions are required.

Appendix B explains the method. Primitives that only MAY be implemented are excluded, with the minimum requirement for inclusion being SHOULD, and excluded primitives are briefly described in their own subsections.
sections.plainLanguage: Locks and secret codes are usually added by another layer, so this list leaves them out, apart from the few services that build in their own.
